title: Expert fanout topology — long-window throughput diagnostics
content:
Summary:
This is a working note from an experimental push to understand throughput regressions we see when serving MoE variants of Llama/Mistral/Qwen with very long contexts (8k–32k). The high-level symptom: steady-state token throughput drops by 12–30% compared to baseline dense runs at the same batch/latency SLO, with degradation worse when per-request context length is highly skewed.

What we measured (quick bullets):
- Multi-model runs: Llama-XL MoE-16, Mistral-MoE-8, Qwen-MoE-32 under identical host config (A100-80GB), same CUDA stack.
- Workloads: synthetic sampler with 1–20k tokens (Pareto tail), real replay from prod trace (anonymized), and oracle-fixed-length sequences (8k, 16k, 32k).
- Metrics captured: per-layer operator times, upstream->GPU memcpy durations, kernel launch latency, per-expert enqueue/dequeue times, KV lookup hits/misses, per-request routing fanout distribution, batch formation fragmentation, and GPU memory watermarking/eviction events.

Repro recipe (minimal)
- Container: rw-infer:experimental-2025-01
- Run harness: scripts/profiles/run_moe_long_context.py --model LlamaXL-moex16 --seq 16384 --qps 40 --clients 16 --trace-id replay-20250112
- Perf capture: nvprof -> nsight-cupti traces + runtime microtraces (rt-trace.log). Use trace-merge.py to synthesize timeline.

Key observations (ordered by impact):
1) Fanout-induced batching fragmentation
   - Routing that fans an input across 4–16 experts creates many small per-expert micro-batches across the same timestep. These micro-batches are not coalesced before kernel dispatch because our batch ID translation logic runs after tokenization/fanout.
   - Result: dozens of kernel launches per timestep with low occupancy; average kernel active SM% drops 18% vs dense.

2) KV cache affinity mismatch
   - Long context keeps large KV caches in GPU; however routing moves tokens to experts that have no warm-up in their local KV segments, causing repeated remote-prefetch patterns in multi-GPU setups (we use tensor-sliced KV).
   - Cache miss cost: synchronous prefetch spikes (20–40ms) on some traces, correlating with major tail latencies.

3) Host->Device transfer jitter and serialization
   - When many small expert requests are enqueued, the host-side loop serializes memcpy + kernel-launch for each micro-batch. On heavy skew, memcpy scheduling jitter introduces 1–3ms noise per micro-batch, accumulating into measurable throughput loss.

4) Per-expert kernel shape variability
   - Experts have different internal FFN shapes (especially in Mistral-derivatives). Kernel selection logic sometimes picks suboptimal kernel (fallback generic kernel) causing a 10–25% slowdown for that expert’s calls.

5) Eviction & UVM interplay (observed on configs using mixed UVM + pinned memory)
   - Long windows push allocation watermarks; occasional GPU page faults appear in nvtx traces when switching between dense and MoE requests. Eviction stalls can cost 30–70ms.

Low-level trace excerpt (representative)
- Request A (16k): routing fanout=6, per-expert micro-batches sizes = [2,1,1,3,2,1] tokens -> 10 kernel launches, memcpy jitter 12ms total, GPU kernel active time 48ms, overhead 28ms, end-to-end step 76ms.
- Baseline dense Request B (16k): single kernel launch, active time 54ms, overhead 6ms, end-to-end step 60ms.

Hypotheses we validated quickly:
- Coalescing micro-batches by expert prior to memcpy reduces host-side jitter and cut overhead by ~40% in the harness (simulated coalescer).
- Early abstraction of batch IDs (create consistent expert->global-batch id map before tokenize) removes the need for late translation and reduces number of kernel launches by up to 30% for fanout>4 cases.
- Adding a small warmup policy (route first N tokens always to default expert) increases KV hit-rate by 8–12% and mainly helps skewed workloads.

Quick experiments & numbers
- Baseline (no coalescing): throughput 820 tok/s at 95ms p50 step time (fanout median 5).
- With coalescing simulation: throughput 1,020 tok/s at 82ms p50 (microbatch kernel count -28%).
- With coalescing + warmup: throughput 1,090 tok/s at 78ms p50 (KV hit-rate +9%).

Immediate actions (short-term)
- Implement a host-side microbatch coalescer that aggregates copies per-expert before issuing GPU memcpy; target PR in the runtime: rw-infer/serving-runtime#coalesce-microbatches (assigned Miguel).
- Add kernel-selection logging gated behind trace flag to capture actual kernel chosen per-expert invocation (Rina).
- Prototype a weighted warmup routing policy that biases first 4 tokens to the hottest expert for each user/session (Daniel).

Open questions / follow-ups
- Multi-GPU tensor layout: would switching from tensor-sliced KV to expert-local replicated KV reduce prefetch cost at acceptable memory overhead? Need cost model test.
- Long-window fairness: Can we detect per-request context skew earlier in the pipeline and preemptively change routing granularity?
- Persistent micro-batch assembly: what is the right TTL for holding micro-batches to wait for coalescing vs latency SLO?

Notes to self / TODOs in the doc
- Capture more production traces with session-level affinity labels (owner: infra-instrumentation).
- Add a microbenchmark for per-expert kernel selection across Mistral->FFN-size param grid.
- Re-run eviction traces with HBM-only mode to isolate UVM impacts (may require infra schedule).

Appendix: quick command outputs
- nvprof sample line: KernelX (expert12) launches 23, avg runtime 2.1ms, occupancy 42%
- rt-trace snippet: [2025-01-12T16:03:10Z] req=abcd fanout=5 microbatches=9 memcpy_host_to_device total=11.8ms kernel-overhead=24.2ms

If you are reading this and want to experiment: start with the coalescer sketch in patches/coalescer-sketch.py (prototype), run with synthetic skewed tails, and plumb kernel-selection logs into the timeline.

Unresolved: small batches that coalesce across different timesteps (temporal coalesce) cause correctness complexity with kv-index offsets — we need invariants defined before implementing across the runtime.

Acknowledgements:
- Thanks to Miguel for the harness and the early coalescer prototype, Rina for kernel selection tracing help, Daniel for routing policy sketches.
